phrases.text: In eighteen twelve, Napoleon marched more than six hundred thousand men into Russia.
Most of them would never come home.
June twenty-fourth.
The Grand Army crosses the Niemen River.
Outnumbered, the Russians do the unexpected.
They retreat.
Mile after mile, they fall back east, burning crops and villages behind them.
Heat, hunger and disease kill tens of thousands on the march.
Then, on September seventh, at Borodino,
the two armies finally collide.
In a single day, around seventy thousand men are killed or wounded.
A week later, Napoleon takes Moscow.
But the city is empty.
And that night, it begins to burn.
He waits five weeks for a surrender that never comes.
On October nineteenth, he orders the retreat.
Then, the Russian winter arrives.
Freezing, starving, and hunted by Cossacks, the army falls apart.
At the Berezina River, thousands more are lost.
Of more than six hundred thousand men, fewer than one in five ever made it back.
